Notation and tool support

DECLARE introduces a variable, SET assigns a value, INPUT reads and OUTPUT displays. Arrays start at index 0. FOR includes its end value. A positive-step range with its start above its end runs zero times. // starts a short comment. Blue keywords, brown strings and green comments use separate styles while following your chosen theme.

Pseudocode is a design notation with different institutional conventions. These examples do not compile directly in Visual Studio. Use the StudyLab tracer for its supported subset. The matrix extension uses supported separate row and column brackets. Some object-oriented designs still require a written trace. A generated flowchart alone does not verify a program's behaviour.

Unit 1 . Core lesson 1

Algorithms and the development life cycle

Learning goals

  • Explain an algorithm and input-process-output.
  • Describe the program development life cycle.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Pseudocode and program structure

Pseudocode is a readable design notation rather than one universal programming language. These examples use a consistent teaching dialect. Indentation shows which statements belong to a block. BEGIN marks the main program entry and END closes it. METHOD and CLASS definitions describe reusable parts outside that main program. Their detailed syntax is introduced in later units. A complete solution states inputs, processing and outputs. A precondition describes assumed valid inputs. Validation is extra logic that checks whether an input satisfies those rules.

Variables declarations and data types

A variable is a named storage location. DECLARE price AS REAL introduces price and its type. A declaration alone does not provide an input value or an initial value in this teaching notation. INTEGER holds whole numbers. REAL allows fractional numbers. STRING holds text. BOOLEAN holds TRUE or FALSE. NUM is a general numeric type for whole numbers and decimals; it does not include text or Boolean values. A parameter is also a declared variable: a method header declares it and a method call supplies its value. A field declaration introduces data belonging to each object.

Initial values and literals

SET price = 20.0 assigns a value to the previously declared price. SET replaces its old value. A later expression reads the value stored at that point in execution. A literal is a value written directly in the code, such as 20.0, 3, TRUE or "Lebo". Literals do not need DECLARE. Quoted text is a STRING literal, while an unquoted identifier names a variable. A constant is a named value that remains fixed after definition. Variables may change. A zero-based index starts at 0. Counting items and identifying positions are different uses of numbers.

Before reading this example

The first program declares price, quantity and total before use. INPUT supplies the two input values. total receives a calculated value before OUTPUT reads it. The literal 3 is the test quantity, not a separate variable name. Text in a prompt describes requirements and is not an executable statement.

What is a program?

A program is a set of instructions that a computer executes. Hardware performs the work; software specifies the instructions. An algorithm is a finite, ordered method for solving a problem. It should be clear enough that each step can be followed without guessing.

Start with the problem

Identify the inputs, the required output and the rules that connect them. For a total price, the inputs might be unit price and quantity; processing multiplies them; output is the total. Distinguish the problem requirements from the programming language used to implement them.

The development life cycle

Analyse requirements, design a solution, implement it, test and debug, deploy it, and maintain it. Documentation accompanies these activities. The cycle is iterative: a failed test may reveal a design issue or an unclear requirement.

Testing a design

Use normal, boundary and invalid data. Compare actual output with an independently calculated expected result. A program that runs without crashing can still produce incorrect results.

What you are building

A shop inputs a non-negative price and quantity. Calculate and display the total. Worked inputs: price = 20 and quantity = 3. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE price AS REAL
  DECLARE quantity AS INTEGER
  DECLARE total AS REAL
  INPUT price
  INPUT quantity
  SET total = price * quantity
  OUTPUT total
END
Check the worked execution
  1. INPUT stores price = 20 and quantity = 3.
  2. The process multiplies the inputs: 20 * 3 = 60.
  3. OUTPUT displays 60. A quantity of 0 gives total 0.

Find and fix the error

Calculate total price as unit price multiplied by quantity. Assume non-negative numeric inputs. 

BEGIN
INPUT price
INPUT quantity
SET total = price + quantity
OUTPUT total
END
Show the repair and explanation 
SET total = price * quantity

The total price is unit price multiplied by the quantity. Adding them does not represent the stated rule.

Try independently

A taxi charges R15 per trip plus R3 for each kilometre. Identify inputs, processing and outputs. Write pseudocode with declarations. Reject a negative distance. Test 0, 4 and -1 km.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Input distance as REAL. Reject distance < 0. Otherwise fare = 15 + 3 * distance and display fare. Expected results: R15, R27 and Invalid distance. Declare fare as REAL. Document the fixed charge as a constant. Do not charge a fare for rejected input.

  • Identify distance and fare
  • Declare numeric data and the fixed charge
  • Check distance before calculation
  • Calculate and output correctly
  • Give all three expected results

Unit 1 . Core lesson 2

Pseudocode and flowchart symbols

Learning goals

  • Explain the purpose of pseudocode.
  • Choose the correct flowchart symbols.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

A condition is a BOOLEAN expression. >= includes the boundary while < excludes it. THEN introduces the true branch and ELSE introduces the false branch. The age or temperature name in each example is declared, then filled by INPUT before its comparison. Only the selected output branch runs.

Pseudocode is a design notation

Pseudocode expresses an algorithm in a readable, language-independent form. There is no single universal syntax. This platform documents its own consistent conventions so that examples and the converter can be checked predictably.

Flowchart symbols

A rounded terminal represents Start or End. A rectangle represents a process, such as a calculation. A parallelogram represents input or output. A diamond represents a decision with labelled branches. Arrows show the direction of execution; they are not decoration.

Represent complete paths

Every decision needs a path for each possible outcome. A loop must have a route back to its condition and a route out. Keep flow direction consistent, label branches and avoid ambiguous crossings.

Readability

Indent statements inside a structure, use meaningful identifiers and pair opening and closing keywords. Comments begin with // in the chart lab. Comments explain a reason or assumption rather than repeat an obvious statement.

What you are building

Input an age. Display Adult for age at least 18 and Minor otherwise. Assume a valid non-negative whole number. Worked input: 18. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE age AS INTEGER
  INPUT age
  IF age >= 18 THEN
    OUTPUT "Adult"
  ELSE
    OUTPUT "Minor"
  ENDIF
END
Check the worked execution
  1. age receives 18. The test 18 >= 18 is TRUE.
  2. Only the first branch runs. Output: Adult.
  3. With age 17, the condition is FALSE and output is Minor.

Find and fix the error

Display Adult when age is at least 18. Close each selection with the matching keyword. 

BEGIN
INPUT age
IF age >= 18 THEN
OUTPUT "Adult"
ENDWHILE
END
Show the repair and explanation 
ENDIF

An IF structure must close with ENDIF in the platform notation. ENDWHILE closes a different structure.

Try independently

Draw a flowchart for a library fine: read days late, reject negatives, charge R2 per day and display the fine. Label each decision exit. Explain which symbols you used.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Use a terminator for Start and End, input/output parallelograms for reading days and showing fine/error, a decision diamond for days < 0 and a process rectangle for fine = days * 2. Yes leads to the error output and No to the calculation. Join both paths before End. At 0 days the fine is R0; at 3 days it is R6.

  • Start and End
  • Input and output symbols
  • Labelled decision
  • Correct process and connected paths
  • Zero and positive tests

Unit 1 . Core lesson 3

Data types, variables and constants

Learning goals

  • Distinguish variables from constants.
  • Choose appropriate data types.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

A declaration chooses a type but does not itself initialise the variable. SET and INPUT provide initial values before expressions read them. REAL can represent fractional values. A STRING identifier preserves leading zeros. BOOLEAN stores a logical state rather than the text "TRUE". FOR repeats a block with a declared counter over inclusive start and end bounds. ENDFOR advances it. A product accumulator starts at 1 so multiplication preserves the supplied factors.

Variables and constants

A variable is a named storage location whose value can change during execution. A constant represents a value that should not change. Choose names that convey meaning, such as numberOfLearners instead of n when context is unclear.

Common data types

NUM stores numeric values, including whole numbers and decimals, for example 7 and 7.5. INTEGER restricts values to whole numbers; REAL also accepts whole numbers and decimals; STRING stores text; BOOLEAN represents TRUE or FALSE. A phone number is often text because leading zeroes and symbols matter and arithmetic is not required.

Initialisation and assignment

Initialisation gives a variable its starting value. Assignment replaces its current value. In this platform SET total = total + price means evaluate the right side using the old total, then store the result on the left.

Type and validation

A type describes the kind of value; validation checks whether a value is acceptable for the problem. An integer age of -4 has the expected type but fails the business rule. Document assumptions about input and conversions.

What you are building

Choose suitable types for a learner identifier, item count, average and active flag. Calculate an average for total = 150 and count = 2. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE learnerId AS STRING
  DECLARE count AS INTEGER
  DECLARE total AS REAL
  DECLARE average AS REAL
  DECLARE active AS BOOLEAN
  SET learnerId = "0017"
  SET count = 2
  SET total = 150.0
  SET active = TRUE
  SET average = total / count
  OUTPUT learnerId, average, active
END
Check the worked execution
  1. STRING preserves the leading zeros in "0017". INTEGER stores the whole-item count 2.
  2. REAL allows a fractional average. Here 150.0 / 2 = 75.0.
  3. BOOLEAN holds TRUE or FALSE. Displayed values: 0017, 75.0, TRUE.

Find and fix the error

Add an input price to an accumulator initialised to zero. Select the line BEFORE which initialisation must be inserted. 

BEGIN
DECLARE total AS REAL
INPUT price
SET total = total + price
OUTPUT total
END
Show the repair and explanation 
SET total = 0, then INPUT price

Before accumulation, initialise total to zero. Keep the original INPUT price after the initialisation.

Try independently

Choose types for learner number 00128, number of books, price and membership status. Explain why a learner number is not an integer. Write declarations and initialise one value of each type.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Use STRING for learner number, INTEGER for a count, REAL for the teaching price and BOOLEAN for membership. DECLARE learnerNumber AS STRING then SET learnerNumber = "00128" preserves leading zeros. Declare books INTEGER and set 3; price REAL and set 42.50; member BOOLEAN and set TRUE. Real financial software may use a decimal money type rather than binary floating point.

  • STRING with leading zeros
  • INTEGER for count
  • REAL for teaching price
  • BOOLEAN for status
  • Declarations and initial values

Unit 1 . Core lesson 4

Expressions and operator precedence

Learning goals

  • Create and evaluate mathematical expressions.
  • Use parentheses to make intent explicit.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

An arithmetic expression produces a value. Parentheses group addition before division in an average. Multiplication and division precede addition without those parentheses. The example uses / for fractional division. DIV means integer quotient and MOD means remainder in this course. Denominators must be nonzero. A percentage means a value divided by 100. A 10% discount is 0.10 of the subtotal, so multiplying by 1 - 0.10 leaves the 0.90 share that must be paid.

Expressions produce values

An expression combines values, variables and operators to produce a result. A statement performs an action, such as assigning that result. For example, price * quantity is an expression; SET total = price * quantity is a statement.

Precedence

In this course, parentheses are evaluated first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Operators at the same arithmetic level are evaluated left to right. Use parentheses to state intent rather than rely on a reader remembering the rules.

Division and remainders

Real division can produce a fraction. DIV denotes integer quotient and MOD the remainder in theory examples. They are useful for divisibility checks and time conversion. The flowchart lab displays expressions but does not evaluate their mathematical correctness.

Checking a result

Trace with small values and calculate the expected result separately. If two marks are 40 and 60, their average is 50. An expression giving 70 has a logic problem even if the syntax is accepted.

What you are building

Read two valid marks and display their average. Worked inputs: 40 and 60. Show why parentheses are necessary. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE mark1 AS REAL
  DECLARE mark2 AS REAL
  DECLARE average AS REAL
  INPUT mark1
  INPUT mark2
  SET average = (mark1 + mark2) / 2.0
  OUTPUT average
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Parentheses first: 40 + 60 = 100.
  2. Then divide: 100 / 2.0 = 50.0. Output: 50.0.
  3. Without parentheses, 40 + 60 / 2.0 would give 70.0.

Find and fix the error

Calculate the average of two marks by dividing their sum by two.

BEGIN
INPUT mark1
INPUT mark2
SET average = mark1 + mark2 / 2
OUTPUT average
END
Show the repair and explanation 
SET average = (mark1 + mark2) / 2

Parentheses make the addition happen before dividing the total by two.

Try independently

Evaluate 18 DIV 4, 18 MOD 4, 3 + 4 * 2 and (3 + 4) * 2. Then write the formula for a weighted mark where test contributes 40% and exam contributes 60%. Use test 70 and exam 80.

Show answer and self-check criteria

The results are 4, 2, 11 and 14. DIV gives the integer quotient for these positive integers and MOD gives the remainder. weighted = test * 0.4 + exam * 0.6 = 28 + 48 = 76. The weights sum to 1.0. Parentheses can clarify intent. Dividing by zero is undefined and must be prevented.

  • DIV and MOD correct
  • Multiplication precedence
  • Parentheses result
  • Weighted expression
  • Result 76 with explanation

Unit 1 . Core lesson 5

Structured design and trace tables

Learning goals

  • Describe sequence, selection and repetition.
  • Identify features of good program design.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

A trace uses the newest value after every SET. The left side is the destination and the right side is evaluated before that destination changes. Sequence, selection and repetition are the basic control structures. The worked assignment trace uses sequence only, so it executes each statement once in order.

Three control structures

Sequence executes statements in order. Selection chooses a path using a condition. Repetition executes a block repeatedly under a control rule. Structured programs combine these patterns into understandable, nested blocks.

Good design

Aim for correctness, clarity, modularity and maintainability. Give each module a clear responsibility, use meaningful names, validate input and reduce unnecessary duplication. A shorter solution is not automatically a clearer or more correct one.

Trace tables

A trace table records changing variable values and output as statements execute. Record the initial state, then each assignment or loop iteration. Evaluate conditions using the current values, not the values you expect later.

Dry run

Manually execute an algorithm using a small test case. Record the actual output and compare it with the expected output. A trace is evidence about that test case, not proof that every possible input works.

What you are building

Trace assignment statements and show the final value of x. Each assignment changes x before the next statement executes. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE x AS INTEGER
  SET x = 3
  SET x = x * 2
  SET x = x + 2
  OUTPUT x
END
Check the worked execution
  1. After SET x = 3: x is 3.
  2. After SET x = x * 2: x is 6. After adding 2: x is 8.
  3. OUTPUT displays 8, not an earlier value.

Find and fix the error

Display the final value of x after all assignments.

BEGIN
SET x = 3
SET y = x + 2
SET x = y * 2
OUTPUT y
END
Show the repair and explanation 
OUTPUT x

The requirement is to display the final x. Here y is 5 and the final x is 10.

Try independently

Trace x = 4; y = x + 3; x = y * 2; y = x - y. Record x and y after each assignment. Then identify one syntax error, one runtime error and one logic error in your own examples.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Rows are (x=4,y=unassigned), (4,7), (14,7), (14,7). The final subtraction reads current x=14 and old y=7, then replaces y. An unmatched ENDIF is a syntax error. Division by zero can cause a runtime error. Adding price and quantity when multiplication is required is a logic error. A trace records actual execution order.

  • Initial unassigned state
  • Four ordered rows
  • Final 14 and 7
  • Three error categories
  • Meaningful examples

Unit 2 . Core lesson 6

Boolean expressions and basic selection

Learning goals

  • Use relational operators.
  • Apply AND, OR and NOT.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

Inclusive limits use >= and <=. An AND expression requires both limit checks to hold. The membership flag in the exercise is a declared BOOLEAN. A Boolean variable can appear directly in IF. Both branches assign due before the final output reads it.

Boolean results

A Boolean expression evaluates to TRUE or FALSE. Relational comparisons include =, <>, <, <=, > and >= in this notation. Use a decision to choose an action based on the result.

AND, OR and NOT

A AND B is true only if both operands are true. A OR B is true if at least one operand is true. NOT reverses a Boolean value. Inclusive OR also allows both operands to be true.

Single and dual alternatives

An IF without ELSE runs its body only when the condition is true. IF/ELSE chooses exactly one of two branches. Use the full condition, such as age >= 18 AND hasID = TRUE, instead of an incomplete comparison.

Boundaries

Check the exact boundary value, as well as values just below and above it. If the pass mark is 50, the test mark >= 50 includes a learner who scores exactly 50.

What you are building

Read a mark and display Valid when it is between 0 and 100 inclusive. Display Invalid otherwise. Worked input: 100. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE mark AS REAL
  INPUT mark
  IF mark >= 0 AND mark <= 100 THEN
    OUTPUT "Valid"
  ELSE
    OUTPUT "Invalid"
  ENDIF
END
Check the worked execution
  1. For mark 100: 100 >= 0 is TRUE and 100 <= 100 is TRUE.
  2. TRUE AND TRUE is TRUE. Output: Valid.
  3. Both boundaries are valid. -1 and 101 are invalid.

Find and fix the error

A mark of 50 or more passes, including exactly 50.

BEGIN
INPUT mark
IF mark > 50 THEN
OUTPUT "Pass"
ELSE
OUTPUT "Not yet passed"
ENDIF
END
Show the repair and explanation 
IF mark >= 50 THEN

A score of exactly 50 must pass. The >= operator includes that boundary.

Try independently

A learner qualifies when mark >= 50 AND attendance >= 80. Give a four-row truth table using marks 49/50 and attendance 79/80. Explain why OR would change the rule.

Show answer and self-check criteria

49,79 is FALSE; 49,80 is FALSE; 50,79 is FALSE; 50,80 is TRUE. AND requires both tests to be true. OR would also accept 49,80 and 50,79 because only one condition needs to hold. Validate mark and attendance within 0 to 100 before classifying.

  • Four combinations
  • Correct AND results
  • Boundary 50 included
  • Boundary 80 included
  • OR comparison and validation

Unit 2 . Core lesson 7

Precedence and nested decisions

Learning goals

  • Apply logical precedence.
  • Create complex and nested selection.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

An ELSEIF is checked only after earlier branches fail. A nested IF has its own ENDIF and is evaluated only when its containing branch is selected. A flag such as approved is declared BOOLEAN and set by INPUT. IF approved tests that stored logical value directly.

Logical precedence

This platform uses NOT before AND before OR, after arithmetic and relational expressions. Parenthesise combined conditions when the intended grouping may be unclear.

Nested selection

A nested decision is an IF inside another branch. Each IF needs its own ENDIF. Follow the outer decision first; only evaluate a nested branch when execution enters it.

Complex selection

Several conditions may be combined in one Boolean expression or organised into nested decisions. For example, an applicant may need both an age requirement and either of two acceptable qualifications.

CASE selection

CASE chooses among explicit values of one expression. Use a default branch when other values need handling. It is useful for a menu; it does not replace every kind of range-based decision.

What you are building

Read a valid mark. Display Distinction at 75 or above, Pass at 50 to 74, otherwise Revise. Worked input: 74. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE mark AS REAL
  INPUT mark
  IF mark >= 75 THEN
    OUTPUT "Distinction"
  ELSEIF mark >= 50 THEN
    OUTPUT "Pass"
  ELSE
    OUTPUT "Revise"
  ENDIF
END
Check the worked execution
  1. 74 >= 75 is FALSE, so continue to ELSEIF.
  2. 74 >= 50 is TRUE, so output Pass. The ELSE branch is skipped.
  3. Boundary outputs: 49 gives Revise, 50 gives Pass, 75 gives Distinction.

Find and fix the error

Allow entry only when age is at least 18 AND the person has ID.

BEGIN
INPUT age
INPUT hasID
IF age >= 18 OR hasID = TRUE THEN
OUTPUT "Entry allowed"
ENDIF
END
Show the repair and explanation 
IF age >= 18 AND hasID = TRUE THEN

Both conditions are required. OR would allow someone who meets only one condition.

Try independently

Write selection for shipping: negative weight is invalid; up to and including 2 kg costs R30; above 2 and up to 5 costs R50; above 5 costs R80. Test -1, 0, 2, 2.1, 5 and 5.1.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Use IF weight < 0 THEN error, ELSEIF weight <= 2 THEN 30, ELSEIF weight <= 5 THEN 50, ELSE 80. Close ENDIF. Outputs are invalid, 30, 30, 50, 50, 80. The question permits zero. Check with the business if zero should instead be rejected. Ordered branches avoid overlapping outcomes.

  • Negative check first
  • Boundary at 2
  • Boundary at 5
  • Final ELSE and output
  • All expected results

Unit 2 . Core lesson 8

Counted loops and accumulators

Learning goals

  • Write counted loops.
  • Use counters and accumulators.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

A FOR header controls the declared counter. Inclusive bounds 1 through 3 mean three iterations. ENDFOR advances it and returns to the bound check. A counter such as passed records events. A running total is an accumulator. Their initial values must be set outside the loop they summarise.

Counted repetition

A FOR loop is useful when the number of repetitions is known. Here FOR i = 1 TO 5 includes both endpoints, so it runs five times. A STEP changes the amount added to the counter.

Counter versus accumulator

A counter tracks occurrences or repetitions. An accumulator combines values, often by addition. Initialise a sum to zero and a product to one before accumulation.

Order matters

Read the current value before using it, update the accumulator after the input, and display the final total after the loop if only one final result is required.

Checking iterations

Trace the first iteration, the last valid iteration and the next condition check. For a negative STEP, the loop condition uses the corresponding descending bound.

What you are building

Input exactly three integers and display their total with a FOR loop. Worked inputs: 2, 3 and 4. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE value AS INTEGER
  DECLARE total AS INTEGER
  DECLARE i AS INTEGER
  SET total = 0
  FOR i = 1 TO 3
    INPUT value
    SET total = total + value
  ENDFOR
  OUTPUT total
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Initial total = 0. Iteration 1 reads 2, so total becomes 2.
  2. Iteration 2 reads 3, so total becomes 5. Iteration 3 reads 4, so total becomes 9.
  3. The inclusive bounds give three iterations. Output: 9.

Find and fix the error

Read three values and display their sum, keeping a running total.

BEGIN
SET total = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 3
INPUT value
SET total = value
ENDFOR
OUTPUT total
END
Show the repair and explanation 
SET total = total + value

Assigning value alone discards the previous total. An accumulator adds the new value to the running total.

Try independently

Read six daily sales values, each assumed non-negative. Calculate total and count days with sales >= 100. Declare variables, initialise both accumulators and show results for 100, 0, 80, 120, 100, 50.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Initialise total = 0 and qualifyingDays = 0 before FOR day = 1 TO 6. Read sales inside the loop, add sales to total and increment qualifyingDays only when sales >= 100. After ENDFOR display total and qualifyingDays. Results: total 450 and qualifyingDays 3. The loop counter counts inputs while the conditional counter counts qualifying days.

  • Declarations and initialisation
  • Exactly six inputs
  • Accumulate each sale
  • Conditional counter
  • Outputs 450 and 3

Unit 2 . Core lesson 9

Conditional loops and priming input

Learning goals

  • Use WHILE and REPEAT/UNTIL.
  • Use sentinel values and priming input.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

The priming input gives the WHILE condition an initial value. The body reads the next value so repetition can terminate. A sentinel is excluded from calculations. Guard an average with count > 0 to prevent dividing by zero when no data was entered.

Pre-test loops

WHILE checks its condition before entering the body. It can execute zero times. Something in the body must be able to change the condition, or the loop may never terminate.

Post-test loops

REPEAT executes the body before checking UNTIL. It runs at least once and stops when the UNTIL condition becomes true. This differs from WHILE, which continues while its condition is true.

Priming input

A priming input is read before a loop so the first condition can be evaluated. Read another value at the end of the body to prepare for the next check.

Sentinel-controlled input

A sentinel is a special value that ends input, such as -1 when valid marks are 0 to 100. Do not accidentally include the sentinel in the total or count. Validate other invalid values separately.

What you are building

Read valid marks until the sentinel -1. Display their average, or No data when the first input is -1. Worked inputs: 10, 20, -1. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE value AS REAL
  DECLARE total AS REAL
  DECLARE count AS INTEGER
  SET total = 0
  SET count = 0
  INPUT value
  WHILE value <> -1 DO
    SET total = total + value
    SET count = count + 1
    INPUT value
  ENDWHILE
  IF count > 0 THEN
    OUTPUT total / count
  ELSE
    OUTPUT "No data"
  ENDIF
END
Check the worked execution
  1. The priming input reads 10. After processing it: total = 10 and count = 1.
  2. After 20: total = 30 and count = 2. The next input -1 stops the loop without being added.
  3. Average = 30 / 2 = 15. If count stays 0, display No data and avoid division by zero.

Find and fix the error

Read and display values until a new input equals the sentinel -1.

BEGIN
INPUT value
WHILE value <> -1 DO
OUTPUT value
SET value = value
ENDWHILE
END
Show the repair and explanation 
INPUT value

A new input allows the condition to change. Assigning value to itself cannot obtain the next value.

Try independently

Read temperatures until 999, excluding the sentinel. Display their average or No data. Explain the priming read and update read. Test 10,20,999 and then 999 alone.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Set total=0 and count=0. Read temperature before WHILE temperature <> 999. Inside, add temperature and increment count, then read another temperature. After the loop divide only if count > 0. The first test averages to 15; the second displays No data. Omitting the update read can make a nonterminating loop. A REPEAT loop executes its body at least once, so it needs a guard before including a sentinel.

  • Priming read
  • Sentinel excluded
  • Update read
  • Guard empty input
  • Both expected results

Unit 2 . Core lesson 10

Nested loops

Learning goals

  • Trace nested loops.
  • Predict the number of body executions.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

The row counter controls outer iterations; column controls the first example and col controls the second example. Both counters are declared independently. matrix[row][col] denotes a declared two-dimensional element. Reset rowTotal for each row before accumulating its values. DECLARE matrix[2][2] AS INTEGER allocates two rows and two columns. Indices 0 and 1 are valid in each dimension. INPUT supplies each selected element before the program adds it to rowTotal.

A loop inside a loop

For each outer-loop iteration, the entire inner loop runs. With three rows and four columns, a simple nested traversal visits twelve cells.

Independent counters

Use separate variables for outer and inner control. Reusing the outer counter inside the inner loop changes the outer-loop state and makes the algorithm difficult to reason about.

Reset at the correct level

Reset a per-row total at the beginning of each outer iteration. Reset a grand total only once before the outer loop. Initialising at the wrong level changes what is accumulated.

Trace one row first

Record the outer counter, inner counter and output for a small example. Count how many times the body executes before generalising to larger bounds.

What you are building

Display each (row, column) pair for rows 1 to 2 and columns 1 to 3.

BEGIN
  DECLARE row AS INTEGER
  DECLARE column AS INTEGER
  FOR row = 1 TO 2
    FOR column = 1 TO 3
      OUTPUT row, column
    ENDFOR
  ENDFOR
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Outputs in order: (1,1), (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (2,2), (2,3).
  2. The inner counter restarts for every outer iteration. There are six pairs.

Find and fix the error

Use independent counters for a two-row, three-column nested loop. Identify the inner header that overwrites the outer counter. 

BEGIN
FOR row = 1 TO 2
FOR row = 1 TO 3
OUTPUT row
ENDFOR
ENDFOR
END
Show the repair and explanation 
FOR column = 1 TO 3

Use a distinct inner counter, such as column. Adjust the body to use row and column as required.

Try independently

A theatre has 3 rows with 4 seats per row. Use nested loops to display each row and seat pair. State first pair, last pair and total outputs. Convert the outer FOR to a WHILE.

Show answer and self-check criteria

FOR row=1 TO 3 contains FOR seat=1 TO 4 and OUTPUT row,seat. Results begin 1,1 and end 3,4 with 12 outputs. For WHILE initialise row=1, use WHILE row <= 3, keep the inner FOR, increment row after ENDFOR and close ENDWHILE. The inner counter starts again for each row.

  • Correct outer range
  • Correct inner range and nesting
  • Output pair
  • 12 with endpoints
  • Equivalent WHILE with update

Unit 3 . Core lesson 11

Arrays and element access

Learning goals

  • Explain an array data structure.
  • Access array elements safely.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

Capacity is the allocated number of elements. A valid zero-based index lies between 0 and capacity - 1. Array values must be supplied before use. Starting a maximum at the first actual element handles all-negative data. Starting it at zero would introduce a value that may not exist in the data.

What an array stores

An array groups values under one name and provides access by index. The values normally share a data type. A fixed-size array has a defined capacity; the number of meaningful values may be smaller than that capacity.

Index convention

This platform uses zero-based indexing: an array with n elements has indices 0 through n - 1. State the convention in a solution. A one-based algorithm is also possible when its bounds are consistently defined.

Traversal

Visit each element using a loop. Never use n as a valid index in a zero-based array of length n. Check array bounds before accessing an element.

Two-dimensional arrays

A two-dimensional array uses row and column indices, such as marks[row][column]. Nested loops traverse the rows and columns. Keep track of both dimensions and their valid ranges.

What you are building

Use a single INTEGER array [1,2,3,4,5]. Calculate its total and average. Show valid indices. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE values[5] AS INTEGER
  DECLARE i AS INTEGER
  DECLARE total AS INTEGER
  SET values[0] = 1
  SET values[1] = 2
  SET values[2] = 3
  SET values[3] = 4
  SET values[4] = 5
  SET total = 0
  FOR i = 0 TO 4
    SET total = total + values[i]
  ENDFOR
  OUTPUT total, total / 5.0
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Valid indices are 0 through 4. Length is 5.
  2. Totals after successive elements: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15.
  3. Output: total 15 and average 3.0.

Find and fix the error

Display all five elements of an already populated array values[5]. Arrays start at index 0. 

BEGIN
FOR i = 0 TO 5
OUTPUT values[i]
ENDFOR
END
Show the repair and explanation 
FOR i = 0 TO 4

For an array of length five, index five is out of bounds. The last valid index is four.

Try independently

For marks [40,75,60,90], calculate the total, average and highest value using a loop. State valid zero-based indexes and explain why initialising highest to 0 is unsafe for arbitrary negative data.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Valid indexes are 0 to 3. Set total=0 and highest=marks[0], then visit indexes 0..3, accumulating and replacing highest when a larger value is found. Total=265, average=66.25, highest=90. For arbitrary all-negative numbers, 0 may not occur and would be an incorrect maximum. A nonempty array is a precondition when using its first element.

  • Valid bounds
  • Initial values
  • Traversal and updates
  • 265,66.25,90
  • Negative and empty reasoning

Unit 3 . Core lesson 12

Linear search

Learning goals

  • Search an array for a specific value.
  • Handle a value that is not found.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

foundAt is a declared index result. Its initial value -1 means no match yet. i is the declared traversal index and target is the declared search value. The loop checks i < length before its body accesses values[i]. Stop after the first match when the requirement asks for its first position.

Search one element at a time

Linear search compares the target with elements in sequence. It works on unsorted arrays and may need to inspect every element.

Track the result

Use a found flag or an index initialised to a value outside the valid index range, such as -1. A match at index zero must not be confused with not found.

Stop appropriately

You can stop at the first match when only one position is needed. Searching for every occurrence requires continuing and recording each match.

Efficiency

In the worst case, linear search examines n elements, written O(n). Search cost grows with the number of elements. This is a broad growth description, not a stopwatch measurement.

What you are building

Find the first position of target 7 in [7,3,7,2]. Stop after the first match and use -1 for no match. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE values[4] AS INTEGER
  DECLARE target AS INTEGER
  DECLARE foundAt AS INTEGER
  DECLARE i AS INTEGER
  SET values[0] = 7
  SET values[1] = 3
  SET values[2] = 7
  SET values[3] = 2
  SET target = 7
  SET foundAt = -1
  SET i = 0
  WHILE i < 4 AND foundAt = -1 DO
    IF values[i] = target THEN
      SET foundAt = i
    ENDIF
    SET i = i + 1
  ENDWHILE
  IF foundAt <> -1 THEN
    OUTPUT foundAt
  ELSE
    OUTPUT "Not found"
  ENDIF
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Initially foundAt = -1 and i = 0. values[0] equals 7, so foundAt becomes 0.
  2. After i becomes 1, foundAt = -1 is FALSE and the loop stops.
  3. Output: 0. It is a valid index and differs from the not-found sentinel -1.

Find and fix the error

Search a populated four-element array for target. Display -1 when absent; otherwise display a matching index. 

BEGIN
SET foundAt = 0
FOR i = 0 TO 3
IF values[i] = target THEN
SET foundAt = i
ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT foundAt
END
Show the repair and explanation 
SET foundAt = -1

Zero is a valid position, so it cannot unambiguously mean not found. Use -1 for this zero-based example.

Try independently

Search [8,3,8,1] for 8 and return the first position. Then search for 9. Explain a not-found sentinel and the number of comparisons in these two cases.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Initialise foundAt=-1 and i=0. While i < 4 and foundAt=-1 compare values[i] to target, record i on a match and increment i. First 8 occurs at index 0 after one comparison. 9 is absent after four comparisons and leaves -1. Never read values[-1]. A last-match search would deliberately continue after a match.

  • Initial state
  • Bounded scan
  • First match retained
  • 0 and -1
  • One/four comparisons and safe access

Unit 3 . Core lesson 13

Parallel arrays

Learning goals

  • Explain related positions in parallel arrays.
  • Keep associated values aligned.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

An index links corresponding records in parallel arrays. names[i] and marks[i] belong to the same student because the data was stored in matching positions. best stores an index, not the largest mark itself. Using that index accesses both the winning name and its mark.

Related records across arrays

Parallel arrays store different attributes in separate arrays, linked by a shared index. names[2] and scores[2] describe the same learner when the arrays are kept aligned.

Search and retrieve

Search one array to find an index, then use that index in the related arrays. Check for not found before using a result index.

Maintain alignment

If you reorder one parallel array, move the corresponding entries in every related array. Sorting only scores would disconnect learners from their marks.

Design alternative

Objects or records can keep related attributes together, reducing alignment errors. Parallel arrays remain useful for understanding indexing and relationships.

What you are building

Store names [Lebo,Naledi,Thabo] and marks [64,81,72] in parallel arrays. Display each matching pair. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE names[3] AS STRING
  DECLARE marks[3] AS REAL
  DECLARE i AS INTEGER
  SET names[0] = "Lebo"
  SET names[1] = "Naledi"
  SET names[2] = "Thabo"
  SET marks[0] = 64
  SET marks[1] = 81
  SET marks[2] = 72
  FOR i = 0 TO 2
    OUTPUT names[i], marks[i]
  ENDFOR
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Index 0 pairs Lebo with 64. Index 1 pairs Naledi with 81.
  2. Index 2 pairs Thabo with 72. Three pairs are displayed.
  3. The same index identifies one record across both arrays.

Find and fix the error

Each name and score at the same index belong to one learner. Display the name and score of learner index 2. 

BEGIN
SET i = 2
OUTPUT names[i], scores[0]
END
Show the repair and explanation 
OUTPUT names[i], scores[i]

Use the same index for related attributes; scores[0] may belong to another learner.

Try independently

names=[Ada,Bo,Cy], marks=[70,90,60]. Find the top learner and display the matching name and mark. If sorting marks descending, explain which other values must move.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Store bestIndex=0, scan indexes 1..2 and replace bestIndex when marks[i] > marks[bestIndex]. Display names[bestIndex] and marks[bestIndex]: Bo 90. Any swap of two marks must swap the names at those same positions. Otherwise names are assigned the wrong results. State a tie rule, such as keeping the first highest mark.

  • Use shared indexes
  • Track best index
  • Comparison and update
  • Bo 90
  • Paired swaps and tie rule

Unit 3 . Core lesson 14

Bubble sort

Learning goals

  • Explain why sorting is useful.
  • Write and trace bubble sort.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

A pass is one traversal of adjacent pairs. j + 1 addresses the right neighbour, so the bound must leave that neighbour inside the array. A swap needs a declared temporary variable. Save the left value before overwriting its slot, then copy the saved value to the right slot.

Why sort?

Sorting puts values into a defined order so they can be read, compared or processed more conveniently. It can support other algorithms, but sorting itself has a cost.

Adjacent comparisons

Bubble sort compares neighbouring values and swaps them when they are in the wrong order. In ascending order, swap when values[j] > values[j + 1]. A temporary variable prevents losing a value.

Passes and bounds

After a full left-to-right pass, the largest remaining value reaches the end of the unsorted part. Shorten later passes. For n elements, a basic implementation needs at most n - 1 passes.

Complexity

The straightforward nested-loop version has O(n squared) comparisons in the worst case. A swapped flag can stop early when a pass makes no swaps. It is useful for learning but usually not the best general sorting choice for large data.

What you are building

Sort [5,2,4,1] into ascending order using bubble sort. Use adjacent comparisons and a temporary variable. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE values[4] AS INTEGER
  DECLARE pass AS INTEGER
  DECLARE j AS INTEGER
  DECLARE temp AS INTEGER
  SET values[0] = 5
  SET values[1] = 2
  SET values[2] = 4
  SET values[3] = 1
  FOR pass = 0 TO 2
    FOR j = 0 TO 2 - pass
      IF values[j] > values[j + 1] THEN
        SET temp = values[j]
        SET values[j] = values[j + 1]
        SET values[j + 1] = temp
      ENDIF
    ENDFOR
  ENDFOR
  OUTPUT values[0], values[1], values[2], values[3]
END
Check the worked execution
  1. After pass 0: [2,4,1,5]. The largest value reaches the right end.
  2. After pass 1: [2,1,4,5]. After pass 2: [1,2,4,5].
  3. Output: [1,2,4,5]. A temporary variable preserves the left value during a swap.

Find and fix the error

Swap the adjacent elements values[j] and values[j + 1]. Assume j and j + 1 are valid indices and both elements contain data. 

BEGIN
SET temp = values[j]
SET values[j] = values[j + 1]
SET values[j + 1] = values[j]
END
Show the repair and explanation 
SET values[j + 1] = temp

The original left value is in temp. Using values[j] again duplicates the right value.

Try independently

Trace ascending bubble sort on [4,1,3,2]. Show the array after each full pass and explain why the inner bound shrinks. Count comparisons for the basic three-pass version.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Pass 1: [1,3,2,4]. Pass 2: [1,2,3,4]. Pass 3: [1,2,3,4]. Comparisons: 3+2+1=6. Each pass settles the largest remaining item at the end, so that position needs no further comparison. Swap adjacent elements only if left > right. A swapped flag permits early exit after a pass with no swaps.

  • Pass 1
  • Pass 2 and 3
  • Six comparisons
  • Bound explanation
  • Safe swap and early exit idea
Open lesson activities and quiz

Unit 4 . Core lesson 15

Decomposition and hierarchy charts

Learning goals

  • Explain methods and modules.
  • Break a program into modules and draw a hierarchy chart.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

Method definitions appear before Main. Main is the BEGIN/END section that calls them. Parameters and return values carry data without an undeclared shared variable. ReadName returns a STRING. Greet receives a declared STRING parameter and returns no value. CALL performs that no-value operation.

One responsibility per module

A method or module is a named unit of work. Decomposition divides a problem into smaller responsibilities, such as reading input, calculating a result and displaying output.

Method headers

A header names the method and describes its parameters. A function also specifies a result type in many notations. A method may return a result when its header declares RETURNS. A method without a result is invoked with CALL. A value-returning method is also called a function in many pseudocode dialects.

Hierarchy charts

A hierarchy chart shows the relationship between a controlling module and the modules it calls. It describes program organisation, not the step-by-step decision paths shown by a flowchart.

Cohesion and coupling

Cohesion is how closely a module’s tasks belong together. Coupling describes dependencies between modules. Prefer focused modules with clear interfaces instead of modules that rely on many unrelated global variables.

What you are building

Decompose a greeting program. ReadName returns a name, Greet receives it, and the main program connects the modules. Worked input: Lebo. 

METHOD ReadName() RETURNS STRING
  DECLARE name AS STRING
  INPUT name
  RETURN name
ENDMETHOD
METHOD Greet(name AS STRING)
  OUTPUT "Hello", name
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
  DECLARE learner AS STRING
  SET learner = ReadName()
  CALL Greet(learner)
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Main calls ReadName. INPUT captures Lebo, which RETURN sends back to learner.
  2. Main calls Greet with learner as the argument. Greet displays Hello, Lebo.
  3. Call hierarchy: Main calls ReadName and Greet. Data moves through return values and parameters.

Find and fix the error

Call the method defined in this program, using its exact name.

METHOD showResult()
OUTPUT "Result ready"
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
CALL showResults()
END
Show the repair and explanation 
CALL showResult()

The call name must match the defined method name in this example.

Try independently

Decompose a shopping receipt into ReadItems, CalculateTotal and DisplayReceipt. Draw a hierarchy chart in words and explain why a hierarchy chart does not show loop decisions.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Main calls ReadItems, CalculateTotal and DisplayReceipt. ReadItems supplies item data, CalculateTotal receives the data and returns a total, DisplayReceipt receives the result to display. Each module has one clear job. A hierarchy chart shows calling structure, whereas a flowchart shows control flow including decisions and repetition. Avoid hidden global data when explicit parameters will do.

  • Main with three child modules
  • Single responsibility
  • Input/data handoff
  • Returned result used
  • Hierarchy versus flowchart
Open lesson activities and quiz

Unit 4 . Core lesson 16

Parameters, arguments and scope

Learning goals

  • Distinguish parameters from arguments.
  • Use methods with and without parameters.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

Parameters are declared in the method header. Arguments are the actual values in a call. The name in a caller is not automatically visible inside a method. Pass-by-value copies the scalar argument. The exercise changes its local number parameter and then shows that the caller counter is unchanged.

Parameters and arguments

A parameter is a placeholder declared in a method header. An argument is the actual value or variable supplied at a call. In displayName(name), name is a parameter in the definition; "Lebo" is an argument in CALL displayName("Lebo").

Passing values

Match argument order, number and compatible types to the method signature. With pass-by-value, the method receives a copy of a value; reassigning the parameter does not reassign the caller’s variable.

Scope

Scope determines where an identifier is accessible. Local variables belong to their method or block. A caller cannot normally read another method’s local variable directly.

No-parameter methods

A method can take no parameters when it needs no caller-supplied values. Avoid replacing clear parameters with unnecessary shared global state.

What you are building

Write DisplayResult with name and mark parameters. Call it with Lebo and 68. Identify parameters versus arguments. 

METHOD DisplayResult(name AS STRING, mark AS REAL)
  OUTPUT name, mark
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
  CALL DisplayResult("Lebo", 68)
END
Check the worked execution
  1. name and mark are formal parameters in the method declaration.
  2. "Lebo" and 68 are arguments supplied by the call, in matching order.
  3. Output: Lebo, 68. Inside the method, name holds Lebo and mark holds 68.

Find and fix the error

displayPair expects two STRING arguments. Supply a first and second name.

METHOD displayPair(first, second)
OUTPUT first, second
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
CALL displayPair("Lebo")
END
Show the repair and explanation 
CALL displayPair("Lebo", "Mpho")

The method expects two arguments. Supply both in the required order.

Try independently

Explain parameters versus arguments using ShowFee(name,fee), called as ShowFee("Lebo",120). If the method changes its local fee under pass-by-value, does the caller's value change? State your assumption.

Show answer and self-check criteria

name and fee are parameter names in the declaration; "Lebo" and 120 are arguments at the call. With value semantics for scalar parameters, the method works with a local copy and assignment does not change a caller variable. A literal cannot be assigned through. Keep local variables inside their declared scope. Reference semantics must be stated separately, especially for arrays/objects.

  • Parameters identified
  • Arguments identified
  • Order/types matched
  • Value-copy assumption
  • Scope and reference distinction
Open lesson activities and quiz

Back to the study route

Unit 4 . Core lesson 17

Functions and return values

Learning goals

  • Write methods that return data.
  • Distinguish returning from displaying.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

RETURNS declares the result type. RETURN supplies the actual value for that invocation and immediately ends it. OUTPUT only displays a value. A returned Boolean can feed IF directly. Each normal path of the Larger method returns an INTEGER, including the equality case.

Return versus output

RETURN passes a result back to the caller and ends that method invocation. OUTPUT displays information. A method that prints a number has not necessarily returned that number for another calculation.

Using a function result

A caller can store a returned value, use it in an expression or pass it to another method. The return type should match the kind of result produced.

All required paths

If a function promises a value, every possible path that finishes normally should return an appropriate value. Missing branches can leave the caller without a defined result.

Converter scope

The chart lab builds control-flow diagrams for its documented statement subset. RETURN is shown as a terminal exit in a method flowchart. Select the method body in the lab to inspect each return path.

What you are building

Write Larger(a,b) returning the larger INTEGER, including equality. Call Larger(8,5), Larger(3,9) and Larger(4,4). 

METHOD Larger(a AS INTEGER, b AS INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  IF a >= b THEN
    RETURN a
  ELSE
    RETURN b
  ENDIF
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
  OUTPUT Larger(8, 5)
  OUTPUT Larger(3, 9)
  OUTPUT Larger(4, 4)
END
Check the worked execution
  1. For (8,5), the TRUE branch returns 8. For (3,9), the FALSE branch returns 9.
  2. For (4,4), equality follows the TRUE branch and returns 4.
  3. Output: 8, 9, 4. Every possible path returns an INTEGER.

Find and fix the error

The add method promises to RETURN the sum to its caller. Select the output statement to replace; displaying alone does not return a value. 

FUNCTION add(a, b) RETURNS REAL
SET result = a + b
OUTPUT result
ENDFUNCTION
Show the repair and explanation 
RETURN result

The function promises a returned value. Displaying the result alone does not fulfil that contract.

Try independently

Write Average(a,b) returning a REAL. Call it for 40 and 75, store the return value and display it. Explain why printing inside Average is insufficient for a caller that needs to make a decision about the result.

Show answer and self-check criteria

METHOD Average(a AS REAL,b AS REAL) RETURNS REAL; RETURN (a+b)/2.0; ENDMETHOD. In Main declare result REAL, SET result=Average(40,75), OUTPUT result. Result=57.5. RETURN supplies a value to the caller; OUTPUT only displays something. The caller can then test result >= 50 or reuse it in another calculation.

  • Typed signature
  • Correct expression
  • RETURN used
  • Call/store/output 57.5
  • Return versus display

Unit 4 . Core lesson 18

Passing arrays to methods

Learning goals

  • Pass an array and its meaningful length.
  • Explain array update assumptions.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

REAL[] or INTEGER[] declares an array parameter. The separately declared count limits processing to meaningful elements, even if capacity is larger. This contract permits count from 0 to capacity. The total method starts its accumulator at zero, so an empty meaningful prefix returns zero.

An array as a parameter

Passing an array lets a method process a collection without duplicating the traversal logic. Include the number of meaningful elements when the array’s capacity may be larger than the data used.

Reference and copy semantics

Whether changes affect the caller depends on the language and the parameter-passing convention. State the assumption in pseudocode. In C#, an array is a reference type: passing the reference by value still permits element updates to the same array.

Respect bounds

Process indices 0 through count - 1 when count is the number of meaningful elements in a zero-based array. Validate that count does not exceed capacity.

Choose a clear contract

Specify what the method receives, what it returns and whether it changes the original elements. Tests should check both the result and any intended changes.

What you are building

Pass an array and a meaningful count to Total. Only the first three elements of [10,20,30,999,999] are data. 

METHOD Total(values AS REAL[], count AS INTEGER) RETURNS REAL
  DECLARE total AS REAL
  DECLARE i AS INTEGER
  SET total = 0
  FOR i = 0 TO count - 1
    SET total = total + values[i]
  ENDFOR
  RETURN total
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
  DECLARE marks[5] AS REAL
  SET marks = [10, 20, 30, 999, 999]
  OUTPUT Total(marks, 3)
END
Check the worked execution
  1. count = 3 produces indices 0, 1 and 2. The running total is 10, then 30, then 60.
  2. The method returns 60, which the caller displays. Spare values 999 are ignored.
  3. Precondition: 0 <= count <= array capacity. At count 0, return the initial total 0.

Find and fix the error

Display count populated elements, starting at index 0. Assume 0 <= count <= array capacity. 

METHOD displayValues(values, count)
FOR i = 0 TO count
OUTPUT values[i]
ENDFOR
ENDMETHOD
Show the repair and explanation 
FOR i = 0 TO count - 1

A zero-based collection containing count values ends at count - 1.

Try independently

Write CountPasses(marks,count) for the first count entries, using pass mark 50. State the contract. Test [50,49,80,999] with count 3, count 0 and count 5.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Require count to be an integer from 0 to capacity inclusive and valid meaningful marks. Initialise passed=0. Loop i=0 TO count-1 and increment when marks[i] >= 50; RETURN passed. count 3 returns 2, count 0 returns 0, count 5 must be rejected because capacity is 4. Do not process unused 999. A zero-length FOR range executes zero iterations in this teaching notation.

  • Count contract
  • Local counter
  • Meaningful range only
  • Conditional increment and return
  • 2,0 and reject
Open lesson activities and quiz

Back to the study route

Unit 4 . Core lesson 19

Overloading and method contracts

Learning goals

  • Explain overloaded methods.
  • Match a call to an appropriate signature.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

A signature uses the method name and parameter list to distinguish operations. Different parameter counts or types create overloads. The full definitions below use declared typed parameters. These examples explain overload selection in writing rather than running inside the diagram lab.

One name, different signatures

Overloading uses the same method name with different parameter lists. The parameter count or types differ. A caller’s arguments determine which compatible overload is selected.

Return type alone is insufficient

In C# and this course’s examples, changing only the return type does not create a valid overload. Parameter names alone do not distinguish overloads either.

Unambiguous design

Use overloads for closely related operations. Avoid combinations that make it unclear which method a call selects. Use meaningful method names when the operations have different responsibilities.

Chart lab limitation

The lab currently requires unique module names. Overload examples belong to the theory and debugging exercises until typed signature resolution is added.

What you are building

Write two Add methods, one for two INTEGER arguments and another for three. Show both calls. Assume the pseudocode dialect supports overloading. 

METHOD Add(a AS INTEGER, b AS INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN a + b
ENDMETHOD
METHOD Add(a AS INTEGER, b AS INTEGER, c AS INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN a + b + c
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
  OUTPUT Add(4, 6)
  OUTPUT Add(4, 6, 2)
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Add(4,6) selects the two-parameter signature and returns 10.
  2. Add(4,6,2) selects the three-parameter signature and returns 12.
  3. Outputs: 10, 12. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads. Written practice: the diagram lab does not resolve overloaded names.

Find and fix the error

Create two distinct overloaded signatures. Parameter names and return type alone cannot distinguish overloads. 

FUNCTION calculate(INTEGER a) RETURNS INTEGER
RETURN a
ENDFUNCTION
FUNCTION calculate(INTEGER b) RETURNS REAL
RETURN b
ENDFUNCTION
Show the repair and explanation 
Change the second header to calculate(REAL b) RETURNS REAL

The original parameter types and count are identical. Change the parameter type or count to create a distinct signature.

Try independently

Define overloaded Perimeter(side) and Perimeter(length,width). Calculate square side 4 and rectangle 4 by 6. Why can changing only a return type fail to distinguish overloads?

Show answer and self-check criteria

Perimeter(side AS REAL) RETURNS REAL returns 4*side; Perimeter(length AS REAL,width AS REAL) RETURNS REAL returns 2*(length+width). Calls produce 16 and 20. Parameter count distinguishes these signatures. Languages such as C# do not use return type alone to choose an overload. State the precondition of non-negative lengths. Overloading differs from overriding an inherited method.

  • One-argument signature
  • Two-argument signature
  • Correct formulas
  • 16 and 20
  • Signature and overriding distinction
Open lesson activities and quiz

Unit 5 . Core lesson 20

Classes, objects and constructors

Learning goals

  • Distinguish a class from an object.
  • Describe attributes and methods.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Access modifiers before the first class example

An access modifier controls where code may directly use a member. PUBLIC allows callers to use that member through the object reference, subject to the language access rules. PRIVATE restricts direct access to the declaring class. Callers use suitable public methods to read or update private fields. This controls program access, rather than encrypting stored data. PROTECTED permits access within the class and its subclasses. It differs from PRIVATE and is useful when discussing inheritance. The worked examples keep their fields private unless a design explicitly needs otherwise.

Before reading this example

PUBLIC and PRIVATE control member access. A constructor is the initialisation operation called when NEW creates an object. The class code now applies those definitions to declared fields and parameters. NEW creates an object, its constructor supplies field values, and the dot calls a public method on that particular object reference.

Class versus object

A class defines a type with data and behaviour. An object is a particular instance of that class. Two Learner objects can have different names while following the same class definition.

State and behaviour

Attributes hold state, such as name and mark. Methods express behaviour, such as calculateAverage. Choose responsibilities that belong to the abstraction being modelled.

Constructors

A constructor initialises a new object into a valid state. It may receive arguments that supply required data. Construction is different from an ordinary method call on an existing object.

Object identity

Two objects can have the same attribute values and still be distinct instances. A reference identifies an object; a class name identifies a type.

What you are building

Create a Book class with a private title, a constructor and a GetTitle method. Construct two objects with different titles and display each title. 

CLASS Book
  PRIVATE title AS STRING
  CONSTRUCTOR Book(value AS STRING)
    SET title = value
  ENDCONSTRUCTOR
  PUBLIC METHOD GetTitle() RETURNS STRING
    RETURN title
  ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
BEGIN
  DECLARE first AS Book
  DECLARE second AS Book
  SET first = NEW Book("Algorithms")
  SET second = NEW Book("Databases")
  OUTPUT first.GetTitle()
  OUTPUT second.GetTitle()
END
Check the worked execution
  1. The first constructor stores Algorithms in the first object. The second stores Databases in another object.
  2. The objects share one class definition but hold separate state.
  3. Outputs: Algorithms, then Databases. This is written OOP notation, outside the flowchart parser grammar.

Find and fix the error

Initialise the name field with the newName parameter supplied by the caller. 

CLASS Learner
PRIVATE name AS STRING
METHOD initialise(newName)
SET name = name
ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
Show the repair and explanation 
SET name = newName

The incoming value should initialise the attribute. Assigning name to itself ignores newName.

Try independently

Design a Student class with private name and mark, a constructor, GetName and HasPassed. Construct Ada with 49 and Bo with 50. Describe separate object state and expected results.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Student stores a STRING name and REAL mark. The constructor accepts and initialises both fields with valid marks in 0..100. GetName returns name and HasPassed returns mark >= 50. Ada.HasPassed() is FALSE and Bo.HasPassed() is TRUE. Each NEW call constructs a separate object with its own fields. A class is the design; an object is one instance. Do not expose unrestricted mark writes.

  • Private typed fields
  • Constructor initialises
  • Methods return values
  • Separate objects/results
  • Validation and encapsulation

Unit 5 . Core lesson 21

Encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism

Learning goals

  • Define the three OOP principles.
  • Choose an appropriate relationship.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

The base Area method is explicitly VIRTUAL. Rectangle marks its implementation OVERRIDE. This makes the permission to replace the inherited implementation visible. Private dimensions are initialised by the Rectangle constructor. The Account exercise controls updates through a public method and a private balance.

Encapsulation

Encapsulation groups data with behaviour and controls access to state. Private attributes and appropriate public methods help preserve valid state. A setter should enforce rules where needed, not merely expose unrestricted changes.

Inheritance

Inheritance defines an is-a relationship: a SavingsAccount is an Account when it fulfils the base contract. A subclass can reuse and specialise behaviour. A has-a relationship is usually represented with composition or association instead.

Polymorphism

Polymorphism allows a common operation to have different implementations depending on the object’s type. A common interface or base type can refer to different concrete objects, and an overridden operation can behave appropriately for each.

Keep the contract

An overriding method should honour the expectations of the common abstraction. Overloading changes parameter signatures; overriding specialises an inherited operation. These are related but distinct ideas.

What you are building

Use a base Shape and a Rectangle subclass. Rectangle stores private dimensions and overrides Area. Call it through a Shape reference to show polymorphism. 

CLASS Shape
  PUBLIC VIRTUAL METHOD Area() RETURNS REAL
    RETURN 0
  ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
CLASS Rectangle INHERITS Shape
  PRIVATE width AS REAL
  PRIVATE height AS REAL
  CONSTRUCTOR Rectangle(w AS REAL, h AS REAL)
    SET width = w
    SET height = h
  ENDCONSTRUCTOR
  PUBLIC OVERRIDE METHOD Area() RETURNS REAL
    RETURN width * height
  ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
BEGIN
  DECLARE shape AS Shape
  SET shape = NEW Rectangle(3, 4)
  OUTPUT shape.Area()
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Inheritance: Rectangle is a Shape. Encapsulation: width and height are private.
  2. The base method is VIRTUAL, so a subclass may override it. A Rectangle object selects the overridden Area even through a Shape reference.
  3. Area = 3 * 4 = 12. Output: 12. The base implementation supplies 0 for a plain Shape in this illustrative design.

Find and fix the error

Protect balance so callers cannot bypass controlled deposit rules. Assume the account balance has already been initialised. 

CLASS Account
PUBLIC balance AS REAL
METHOD deposit(amount)
IF amount > 0 THEN
SET balance = balance + amount
ENDIF
ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
Show the repair and explanation 
PRIVATE balance AS REAL, with controlled access methods

Unrestricted public balance allows callers to bypass the deposit rules. Encapsulation controls updates through an appropriate interface.

Try independently

Choose inheritance or association for Student/Course and SavingsAccount/Account. Explain encapsulation and demonstrate how two child classes can supply different implementations of one inherited operation.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Student has an association with Course because a student is not a course. SavingsAccount can inherit Account if it meets the Account contract. Encapsulation keeps fields private and changes controlled by methods. For polymorphism, Circle and Rectangle can override Shape.Area; calling Area through a Shape reference uses the object's matching override. Overriding uses the inherited contract, unlike different parameter lists in overloading.

  • Student/Course association
  • Account is-a reasoning
  • Encapsulation
  • Override example
  • Runtime dispatch versus overload

Unit 5 . Core lesson 22

Class diagrams and class organisation

Learning goals

  • Draw a class diagram.
  • Describe associations and class responsibilities.
Read the step-by-step explanations

Before reading this example

The Course class is defined before a variable or field uses Course as a type. The Learner constructor declares both of its incoming parameters. Both name and course are assigned during construction before DisplayDetails reads them. The association diagram describes that same relationship.

The three compartments

A basic UML class box has a class name, attributes and operations. Attributes show names and types; operations show parameters and return types where relevant. Use consistent visibility notation: + is public and - is private.

Relationships

An association describes a connection between objects. Inheritance uses a solid line with a hollow triangle pointing to the more general class. Multiplicity describes how many objects participate, such as 1 or 0..*.

Organising classes

Group related responsibilities into cohesive classes. Use association or composition for has-a relationships, inheritance for justified is-a relationships and interfaces for shared contracts. Avoid a single class doing every task.

Class versus hierarchy chart

A class diagram models types, responsibilities and relationships. A hierarchy chart models procedural decomposition. A flowchart models control flow. Choose the diagram that answers the question being asked.

What you are building

Model a Learner associated with a Course. Define both classes. The Learner constructor must initialise both name and course before DisplayDetails can read them. Create the objects and display the result. 

CLASS Course
  PRIVATE title AS STRING
  CONSTRUCTOR Course(value AS STRING)
    SET title = value
  ENDCONSTRUCTOR
  PUBLIC METHOD GetTitle() RETURNS STRING
    RETURN title
  ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
CLASS Learner
  PRIVATE name AS STRING
  PRIVATE course AS Course
  CONSTRUCTOR Learner(value AS STRING, enrolledCourse AS Course)
    SET name = value
    SET course = enrolledCourse
  ENDCONSTRUCTOR
  PUBLIC METHOD DisplayDetails()
    OUTPUT name, course.GetTitle()
  ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
BEGIN
  DECLARE course AS Course
  DECLARE learner AS Learner
  SET course = NEW Course("PRLD")
  SET learner = NEW Learner("Lebo", course)
  CALL learner.DisplayDetails()
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Create the Course with title PRLD first. Pass that declared object reference into the Learner constructor together with Lebo.
  2. The constructor initialises name and course. DisplayDetails can therefore read both fields safely. Output: Lebo, PRLD.
  3. The two classes have an association: Learner has a Course. They do not use inheritance. Each parameter is declared in its constructor header.

Find and fix the error

Draw inheritance from SavingsAccount to its superclass Account. Identify the direction of the hollow triangle. 

Class diagram: SavingsAccount inherits Account
Inheritance triangle points to SavingsAccount
Show the repair and explanation 
Point the hollow triangle to Account

The inheritance triangle points toward the more general superclass, Account.

Try independently

Draw a class diagram for Course(code,title) and Student(name,course). Show private fields and public constructors/GetName methods. Assume each student takes one course and each course has zero or more students. Label multiplicities.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Use class boxes with name, fields and operations. Prefix private fields with - and public operations with +. Course has code:STRING,title:STRING; Student has name:STRING,course:Course. At the Course end of the association write 1, and at the Student end write 0..*. State this simplified business rule; actual registration systems often allow many courses per student and use an Enrolment class. Associations describe links, not inheritance.

  • Class compartments
  • Typed fields and visibility
  • Public operations
  • 1 and 0..* at correct ends
  • Business assumption and association

Unit 2 . Extension 1

SWITCH and menu choices

Learning goals

  • Choose a suitable multi-way selection structure
  • Handle an unknown menu choice
Read the step-by-step explanations

One choice several exact values

Multi-way selection compares one expression with listed exact values. The idea is often called SWITCH. StudyLab writes CASE choice OF, followed by WHEN 1:, WHEN 2: and OTHERWISE:, then ENDCASE. Use it for exact choices such as menu options. IF is usually clearer for ranges. OTHERWISE handles a choice with no matching WHEN. One matching branch runs without falling into the next branch. Other languages use different syntax.

Before the code

Build a tiny menu that displays a course fee. The student enters 1 or 2. Any other integer displays Unknown choice. This example assumes the input has already been converted to an integer. Input conversion and selection are separate responsibilities.

What you are building

Input 1 for a R500 SQL course or 2 for a R600 Docker course.

BEGIN
  DECLARE choice AS INTEGER
  INPUT choice
  CASE choice OF
    WHEN 1:
      OUTPUT 500
    WHEN 2:
      OUTPUT 600
    OTHERWISE:
      OUTPUT "Unknown choice"
  ENDCASE
END
Check the worked execution
  1. choice=2 matches WHEN 2: and displays 600.
  2. The first branch and OTHERWISE do not run.
  3. choice=3 matches no listed value and displays Unknown choice.

Try independently

Add WHEN 3: for a R700 C# course and explain why OTHERWISE must remain. Test 3 and 0.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Insert WHEN 3: followed by OUTPUT 700 before OTHERWISE:. Choice 3 displays 700. Choice 0 displays Unknown choice. OTHERWISE is still needed because unlisted choices remain possible.

  • Read integer choice
  • Three distinct WHEN values
  • Correct fee mapping
  • OTHERWISE remains
  • Tests 3 and 0

Unit 3 . Extension 2

Two dimensional arrays and row totals

Learning goals

  • Read and trace a row and column index
  • Calculate row totals with nested loops
Read the step-by-step explanations

A table of related values

A two dimensional array uses two indexes, such as marks[row][column]. The first selects a row and the second selects a column. For two students taking three tests there are 2 * 3 = 6 elements. Zero based row indexes are 0..1 and column indexes are 0..2. A row total must restart at zero for each new student.

Before the code

Build a report with one total per student. Student 0 has 50,60,70 and student 1 has 80,40,60. The example assigns all six values before reading them. StudyLab uses separate brackets for each dimension: DECLARE marks[2][3] AS REAL and marks[row][column]. You can test this matrix example in the browser tracer.

What you are building

Find each student's total over three tests. Keep the column count separate from the row count. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE marks[2][3] AS REAL
  DECLARE row AS INTEGER
  DECLARE column AS INTEGER
  DECLARE rowTotal AS REAL
  SET marks[0][0] = 50
  SET marks[0][1] = 60
  SET marks[0][2] = 70
  SET marks[1][0] = 80
  SET marks[1][1] = 40
  SET marks[1][2] = 60
  FOR row = 0 TO 1
    SET rowTotal = 0 // Restart for this row
    FOR column = 0 TO 2
      SET rowTotal = rowTotal + marks[row][column]
    ENDFOR
    OUTPUT row, rowTotal
  ENDFOR
END
Check the worked execution
  1. Row 0 visits columns 0,1,2 and totals 50,110,180.
  2. Row 1 starts again at 0 and totals 80,120,180.
  3. Output pairs are (0,180) and (1,180). The inner body runs six times.

Try independently

Modify the report to display row averages and a total for each column. Give all expected results for the shown data.

Show answer and self-check criteria

Display rowTotal/3.0 after each row loop: 60 and 60. For column totals put the column loop outside a row loop, reset columnTotal before scanning its two rows and accumulate marks[row][column]. Column totals are 130,100,130. Bounds stay rows 0..1 and columns 0..2.

  • Correct row averages
  • Separate column total
  • Reset once per column
  • Correct bounds
  • 130,100,130

Unit 5 . Extension 3

Integrated student marks project

Learning goals

  • Combine input validation arrays methods and selection
  • Plan an independent test set and explain a class design
Read the step-by-step explanations

What you are building

Build a marks report for three students. Keep a name and a valid mark for each student. Show each name, mark and result; calculate the class average; find the top student. Use parallel arrays first, then describe how a Student class could keep each name and mark together. The main goal is to make data flow and rules visible.

Build the project in parts

Part 1 declares and fills the arrays. Part 2 validates marks from 0 to 100. Part 3 counts passes using mark >= 50. Part 4 calculates the average after all three inputs. Part 5 tracks the best index and prints its matching name. A separate extension moves classification into a returning method. Only read a variable after assigning it.

Testing the whole report

Use Ada=50, Bo=49 and Cy=75. Expected average is 58, two students pass and Cy is top. Test all zeros, all hundreds and equal top marks. This design keeps the first top student by using > rather than >=. Reject a negative mark and 101, then enter a replacement. The program accepts exactly three valid records, even if it must ask again.

What you are building

The complete main program below combines the parts. Numeric input conversion is assumed; range validation is explicit. Define names and marks before the main report loop. 

BEGIN
  DECLARE names[3] AS STRING
  DECLARE marks[3] AS REAL
  DECLARE i AS INTEGER
  DECLARE total AS REAL
  DECLARE passed AS INTEGER
  DECLARE bestIndex AS INTEGER
  SET total = 0
  SET passed = 0
  SET bestIndex = 0

  FOR i = 0 TO 2
    INPUT names[i]
    INPUT marks[i]
    WHILE marks[i] < 0 OR marks[i] > 100 DO
      OUTPUT "Enter a mark from 0 to 100"
      INPUT marks[i]
    ENDWHILE
    SET total = total + marks[i]
    IF marks[i] >= 50 THEN
      SET passed = passed + 1
      OUTPUT names[i], marks[i], "Pass"
    ELSE
      OUTPUT names[i], marks[i], "Revise"
    ENDIF
    IF marks[i] > marks[bestIndex] THEN
      SET bestIndex = i
    ENDIF
  ENDFOR

  OUTPUT "Average", total / 3.0
  OUTPUT "Passed", passed
  OUTPUT "Top", names[bestIndex], marks[bestIndex]
END
Check the worked execution
  1. After Ada: total=50,passed=1,bestIndex=0.
  2. After Bo: total=99,passed=1,bestIndex=0.
  3. After Cy: total=174,passed=2,bestIndex=2. Average=58.

Try independently

Refactor the classification into Result(mark) returning a STRING. Give the complete method and the calling statement. Then propose private fields and methods for a Student class.

Show answer and self-check criteria

METHOD Result(mark AS REAL) RETURNS STRING; IF mark >= 50 THEN RETURN "Pass" ELSE RETURN "Revise" ENDIF; ENDMETHOD. Place it outside Main. In the report call OUTPUT names[i],marks[i],Result(marks[i]). Precondition: mark already validated. Student has private name STRING and mark REAL; a constructor checks the mark range, GetName returns the name and Result returns the classification. Keep the main report responsible for aggregation across students.

  • Typed returning method
  • Both branches return
  • Call supplies current mark
  • Class fields and constructor
  • Separation of object and class totals
